## Abstract

Severe congenital neutropenia (SCN) is a life-threatening disorder most often caused by dominant mutations of ELANE that interfere with neutrophil maturation. We conducted a pooled CRISPR screen in human hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) that correlated ELANE mutations with neutrophil maturation potential. Highly efficient gene editing of early exons elicited nonsense-mediated decay (NMD), overcame neutrophil maturation arrest in HSPCs from ELANE mutant SCN patients, and produced normal hematopoietic engraftment function. Conversely, terminal exon frameshift alleles that mimic SCN-associated mutations escaped NMD, recapitulated neutrophil maturation arrest, and established an animal model of ELANE mutant SCN. Surprisingly, only −1 frame indels impeded neutrophil maturation, while −2 frame late exon indels repressed translation and supported neutrophil maturation. Gene editing of primary HSPCs allowed faithful identification of variant pathogenicity to clarify molecular mechanisms of disease and encourage a universal therapeutic approach to ELANE mutant neutropenia, returning normal neutrophil production and preserving HSPC function.

## Abstract

Rao and colleagues perform comprehensive gene editing in human primary cells to associate ELANE mutations with neutrophil maturation potential. Indels that trigger nonsense mediated decay (NMD) circumvent severe congenital neutropenia (SCN) mutations. Indels that escape NMD model SCN by xenograft although −2 frame indels repress translation and enable neutrophil maturation.

## INTRODUCTION

In the current era of bountiful human sequencing data (Karczewski et al., 2020), the growing catalog of human genomic variation often resists easy interpretation. A major challenge is to correlate genetic sequence variants with functional outcomes to understand pathogenicity and molecular mechanisms of disease. As gene therapies mature (Dunbar et al., 2018), the inverse problem becomes equally important, to determine which sequence changes could overcome pathogenicity and ameliorate disease. Gene editing in relevant human cell contexts is a promising approach to explore molecular pathophysiology and potential therapies. For most human blood disorders, HSCs, which maintain blood cell production throughout life, are the critical cells that when modified could either produce or rectify disease. Current methods of genome editing based on CRISPR technologies may yield highly efficient and specific gene modifications in human HSCs (Schiroli et al., 2019; Vakulskas et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019). These methods typically require bespoke design, implementation and readout of individual gene edits and do not easily scale to test many perturbations. Pooled screens are a powerful approach to generate numerous genotype-phenotype correlations in parallel. These screens are often conducted with simplified phenotypes and in cell lines where delivery of the gene editing components is easily controlled. One previous report described a method to perform pooled sgRNA screens in primary HSPCs (Ting et al., 2018). However, this approach, termed Guide Swap, in which Cas9 protein along with a nontargeting sgRNA as ribonucleoprotein are delivered along with a pooled sgRNA library by lentiviral transduction was only demonstrated in HSPCs for screens with strong positive selective pressure. Therefore, the feasibility to screen in primary HSPCs for complex phenotypes of modest selective pressure, such as cell differentiation, remains uncertain.

Severe congenital neutropenia (SCN) is a rare inherited disease that impairs neutrophil maturation and results in extremely low circulating neutrophil counts (Skokowa et al., 2017). This blood disorder leads to life-threatening infections in infancy in the absence of specific therapy. Most patients respond to palliating granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) therapy, requiring lifelong treatment with regular subcutaneous infusions. Nonetheless, in these patients there remains a predisposition to myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukemia, with 22% transformation after 15 years on G-CSF therapy (Rosenberg et al., 2006, 2010). The only curative option is allogeneic HSC transplantation, which is limited by donor availability and immune incompatibility with risk of graft rejection and graft-versus-host-disease.

Mutations of the ELANE gene (encoding neutrophil elastase) are the most frequent cause of SCN, accounting for about half of cases (Horwitz et al., 2013; Skokowa et al., 2017). ELANE mutations also cause the related milder disorder cyclic neutropenia. A common feature of ELANE mutations is their dominant nature, where most SCN-associated ELANE mutations are missense. Production of an abnormal neutrophil elastase protein results in neutropenia despite the presence of one intact ELANE allele. Frameshift mutations associated with SCN (Germeshausen et al., 2013) are restricted to distal penultimate exon 4 and final exon 5. These frameshift mutations would be predicted to escape nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) based on the 50 nt rule (Lindeboom et al., 2016, 2019). Similar to missense mutations, NMD-escape mutations would be expected to give rise to an abnormal neutrophil elastase protein. A leading model suggests that abnormal neutrophil elastase proteins cause an unfolded protein response that ultimately results in apoptosis of neutrophil precursors at the promyelocyte-to-myelocyte transition (Grenda et al., 2007; Horwitz et al., 2007; Köllner et al., 2006; Nayak et al., 2015).

CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing systems enable programmable targeting of the Cas9 endonuclease to specific genomic sequences in primary human cells. Here we investigated Cas9-meditated dense mutagenesis in human HSPCs as a means to dissect ELANE neutropenia pathogenicity. We developed a CRISPR/Cas viral co-delivery system to perform a pooled sgRNA screen in HSPC-derived primary neutrophil cultures and identified gene edits that both produce and bypass neutrophil maturation arrest. We confirmed that generation of NMD-triggering ELANE frameshift alleles could be a generalized therapeutic gene editing strategy in HSCs to relieve neutrophil maturation arrest (Nasri et al., 2020). We validated potentially therapeutic ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) in SCN patient primary cells. Using mouse xenografts, we established an animal model of ELANE mutant SCN and demonstrated induction and rescue of ELANE-mediated neutrophil maturation arrest in vivo in HSCs. We discovered based on experimental gene edits and then substantiated with human mutation analysis that different NMD-evading ELANE frameshifts have unique phenotypic consequences, indicating translational regulation of NE expression.

## RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

To investigate the relationship between genetic variation at ELANE and neutrophil maturation potential, we performed an agnostic dense mutagenesis CRISPR screen of ELANE in HSPCs (Fig. 1A). We included all possible ELANE targeting spacer sequences for SpCas9 guide RNAs as restricted by the availability of the NGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) that delimits genomic cleavage. Inefficient transduction by SpCas9 encoding lentiviral vectors has limited the feasibility of pooled SpCas9 based screens in primary human CD34+ HSPCs (Ting et al., 2018). Therefore we used a recently developed temperature-sensitive non-integrating Sendai virus system to achieve efficient SpCas9 delivery to CD34+ HSPCs (Jin et al., 2003; Park et al., 2016). We delivered sgRNAs by lentivirus (LV) to facilitate quantification of integrants. We observed dose-dependent transient infection of human mobilized peripheral blood CD34+ HSPCs, with >95% selection-free infection frequency by ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9 at the permissive temperature (Fig. S1A–C). Enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) expression persisted for at least one week after shifting cells to the restrictive temperature, consistent with protracted Cas9 exposure (Fig. S1D). We found sequential transduction with LV-sgRNA and infection with ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9, including puromycin selection for sgRNA integrants, yielded 79–91% on-target editing after 5 days without additional selection (Fig. S1E). Neutrophil maturation efficiency was similar as compared to uninfected cells (Fig. S1F–G).

We designed an LV sgRNA library composed of 186 ELANE-targeting sgRNAs. We included 100 neutral locus genome targeting sgRNAs as negative controls and 44 gene targeting sgRNAs as positive controls (Fig. 1B). The positive controls comprised 10 genes associated with congenital neutropenia plus CEBPA, a known critical transcription factor for neutrophil development, with 4 sgRNAs per gene. Severe congenital neutropenia is typically associated with neutrophil maturation arrest at the promyelocyte-to-myelocyte stage of neutrophil development. Therefore, we postulated that gene editing of congenital neutropenia genes would result in relative enrichment of gene edits in promyelocytes and relative depletion from neutrophils.

Following sequential transduction of HSPCs with LV-sgRNA and transient infection with ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9, we performed neutrophil maturation culture, and then physically separated by flow sorting promyelocyte-enriched (CD34−CD117+CD16−) and neutrophil-enriched (CD34−CD117−CD16+) populations. Genomic DNA was isolated, sgRNA libraries amplified and sequenced, and relative enrichment of each sgRNA calculated in the promyelocyte compared to neutrophil population (as log2 fold change, L2FC), achieving low multiplicity of infection (MOI) and robust cellular representation (Fig. S1H–I). We found that sgRNAs targeting 9 of 11 positive control genes were significantly enriched in promyelocytes relative to neutrophils (P < 0.01, Fig. 1C), indicating that gene edits targeting congenital neutropenia genes resulted in neutrophil maturation arrest. Notably, of the two exceptions, G6PC3 mutations have been associated with variable neutrophil maturation defects in the bone marrow (Banka et al., 2011; Boztug et al., 2009; McDermott and Eppert, 2010), and VPS45 mutations are associated with marrow fibrosis but not neutrophil maturation arrest (Shah et al., 2017; Vilboux et al., 2013). We found that consistent with prior reports (Doench et al., 2014a; Wang et al., 2014), sgRNA spacer sequences with ≥80% GC content showed diminished editing (Fig. S1J–L). In the context of hematopoietic differentiation, these sgRNAs were associated with more efficient neutrophil maturation, perhaps by minimizing the transient DNA damage response and cell cycle arrest elicited by most gene edits including the neutral locus controls (Haapaniemi et al., 2018; Schiroli et al., 2019). Therefore, we excluded from further analysis sgRNA spacers with ≥80% GC content. We mapped the L2FC promyelocyte/neutrophil enrichment scores for each of the remaining ELANE targeting sgRNAs to the expected position of cleavage within the gene sequence and performed LOESS regression to interpolate enrichment scores across ELANE (Fig. 1D). The greatest promyelocyte enrichment was found over distal exons 4 and 5. The onset of this area of marked enrichment corresponded to the region of ELANE expected to escape NMD based on the 50 nt rule (Lindeboom et al., 2016). Strikingly, this region of gene editing-associated promyelocyte enrichment overlapped the positions where 23 unique dominantly inherited ELANE frameshift mutant alleles have been associated with congenital neutropenia (Germeshausen et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015). Frameshift mutations outside of distal exon 4 and exon 5 have not been associated with congenital neutropenia. Consistent with this observation of human genetics, we found minimal promyelocyte enrichment at the remainder of ELANE. These results suggested that gene edits targeting positions upstream of the 50 nt rule position in exons 1–4 (which we subsequently refer to as early exon editing) in ELANE elicit NMD and thus bypass neutrophil maturation arrest, consistent with a recent report (Nasri et al., 2020). In contrast, gene edits targeting positions downstream of the 50 nt rule position in exons 4–5 (i.e. late exon editing) produce frameshift mutations that fail to elicit NMD, similar to the dominantly inherited frameshift mutations that have been associated with congenital neutropenia.

In order to validate this gene edited model of SCN, we edited human HSPCs by electroporation of 3xNLS-SpCas9:sgRNA RNP followed by neutrophil maturation culture with G-CSF. We targeted a neutral locus or an ELANE early or late exon position (ELANE e2-C71 and e5-R220, nomenclature indicates exon targeted and codon cleaved). Each of the ELANE targeting sgRNAs yielded highly efficient gene edits (96.7% and 94.8% indels respectively, Fig. 2A). ELANE e5-R220 editing only produced modest reduction in ELANE mRNA without selective loss of frameshift alleles in the transcript as compared to the genomic DNA, consistent with escape from NMD (Fig. 2B–C). Editing in exon 5 resulted in neutrophil maturation arrest at the promyelocyte/myelocyte stage, leading to many fewer mature neutrophils (Fig. 2D–E). This abnormality, as measured by both immunophenotype and cell morphology, appears similar to the differentiation block observed in SCN. In contrast, ELANE early exon editing resulted in efficient NMD, with 86.2% reduction in the overall mRNA level, and 3.6-fold reduction of frameshift alleles in the residual mRNA, comparing indels in transcript to genomic DNA (Fig. 2B–C, Table S1). Editing in exon 2 did not impact the efficiency of neutrophil maturation as determined by immunophenotype and cell morphology (Fig. 2D).

We tested 3 additional sgRNAs targeting predicted NMD triggering positions in ELANE early exons and 8 additional sgRNAs targeting predicted NMD escape positions in ELANE late exons that overlap sites of congenital neutropenia associated ELANE frameshifts (Fig. S2). For early exon targeting sgRNAs, there was a strong negative correlation between ELANE indels and mRNA expression level, consistent with NMD. On the contrary, for late exon targeting sgRNAs, there was no relationship between ELANE indels and mRNA expression level and frameshift alleles were largely preserved in mRNA. Only late exon editing resulted in impaired neutrophil maturation. Together these data show that the general impact of introducing PTCs to early exons of ELANE is to trigger NMD while preserving neutrophil maturation potential, whereas PTCs at late exons of ELANE block neutrophil maturation without NMD and only modestly impact ELANE expression. Of note, ELANE expression itself varies during neutrophil maturation (Fig. S2E). Therefore, small changes in ELANE expression in an asynchronous population of maturing neutrophils might reflect maturation kinetics rather than gene regulation per se.

We tested additional 5 sgRNAs in exon 2 that were associated with promyelocyte enrichment in the screen (ELANE e2-G23, e2-A40, e2-F43, e2-F64, e2-M66), albeit the effect for each was more modest than the effect of ELANE e5-R220 (Fig. S3A). We validated that editing with 4 of these 5 sgRNAs led to a statistically significant decrease in neutrophil expansion in vitro, although the effect sizes were smaller as compared to ELANE e5-R220 edited cells (Fig. S3B). We found that each of these produced a mixture of frameshift, inframe and unedited alleles, with the fraction of frameshifts directly proportional to the induction of NMD (Fig. S3C–D). We infer that the nature and frequency of inframe indels determines the impact of early exon gene editing on neutrophil maturation potential.

The maturation arrest in SCN is associated with elevated apoptotic cell death of neutrophil precursors (Bartels et al., 2016). Annexin V staining showed that ELANE e5-R220 editing resulted in increased apoptosis specifically in promyelocyte and myelocyte enriched populations (CD34−CD117+/−CD16−) (Fig. 3A, S3E). One of the hallmark clinical features of SCN is partial neutrophil response to pharmacologic G-CSF. Increasing concentrations of G-CSF, ranging from 1 to 30 ng/ml, were associated with substantially increased neutrophil output from HSPC differentiation cultures (Fig. 3B, S3F–G). Neutrophil output from ELANE late exon position (e4-V190 #2, e5-L206 #1 and e5-R220) targeted HSPCs increased in a dose-dependent manner based on G-CSF concentration, albeit with final neutrophil output diminished at each concentration relative to neutral locus or ELANE e2-C71 editing (Fig. 3B, S3G). Previous studies have demonstrated that in SCN, mutant NE triggers an unfolded protein response (UPR) (Grenda et al., 2007; Horwitz et al., 2007; Köllner et al., 2006; Nayak et al., 2015). Consistent with these findings, we observed an approximately 2-fold increase of the UPR pathway genes BIP and ATF6 in promyelocytes after ELANE e4-V190 #2, e5-L206 #1 and e5-R220 editing (Fig. 3C, S3H–I). Increased concentration of G-CSF did not prevent BIP and ATF6 induction confirming that G-CSF acts downstream of the UPR (Nayak et al., 2015). Together these results suggest that editing within a late exon of ELANE recreates key features of SCN whereas editing within an early exon leads to NMD-triggering premature termination codons (PTCs) that avoid the neutrophil maturation arrest observed in SCN.

We introduced together in healthy donor HSPCs late exon PTCs mimicking SCN associated mutations and early exon PTCs triggering NMD to model the therapeutic potential of early exon ELANE gene editing. Co-delivery of two sgRNAs as an RNP complex produced efficient interstitial deletion between cleavage sites as expected. However, sequential delivery of late exon targeting ELANE e5-R220 and early exon targeting ELANE e2-C71 separated by at least 24 hours resulted in highly efficient indels (>90% at each ELANE position) while avoiding interstitial deletion (Fig. 4A, S4A–C). Editing the early exon of ELANE resulted in similar transcript decay irrespective of late exon editing and markedly reduced the promyelocyte induction of BIP and ATF6 induced by late exon editing (Fig. 4B, Fig. S4D–E). Early exon editing bypassed the neutrophil maturation arrest associated with late exon editing (Fig. 4C, S4F).

ELANE mutations impacting the canonical translation initiation sequence or ribosome binding sequences may promote translation from downstream in-frame initiation codons, yielding amino-terminally truncated NE isoforms, predominantly initiating from two codons in exon 2 called ATG2 and ATG3 (Tidwell et al., 2014). ELANE e2-C71 editing produces indels downstream of ATG3. We tested RNP delivery with two additional sgRNAs, ELANE e2-E29 targeting upstream of ATG2 and ELANE e2-H70 targeting downstream of ATG3 (Fig. S4G). Both also efficiently produced indels, triggered NMD of mutant ELANE mRNA and rescued neutrophil maturation potential (Fig. S4H–M). Immunoblot of NE with an antibody recognizing a carboxyl-terminal epitope showed reduction of full-length NE after ELANE e2-C71, e2-E29, or e2-H70 editing was not accompanied by compensatory expression of amino-terminally truncated NE isoforms (Fig. S4N).

We obtained HSPCs from a patient with SCN carrying the ELANE p.P139L mutation (Fig. S5A). RNP editing with ELANE e2-C71 yielded highly efficient on-target editing and loss of ELANE mRNA expression, similar to that in healthy donor samples (Fig. 4D–E). Upon in vitro neutrophil differentiation, few mature neutrophils were observed in the patient-derived cell cultures (Fig. 4F–G). ELANE early exon targeting efficiently rescued neutrophil maturation arrest, leading to neutrophil expansion with efficiency comparable to healthy donors (Fig. 2E, 4G). We found similar results in three additional congenital neutropenia patients (with ELANE p.L84P and p.I118N missense mutations as well as p.M1del which ablates the canonical translation initiation codon) following editing in ELANE exon 2—induction of NMD and amelioration of neutrophil expansion based on both immunophenotype and morphology (Fig. S5B–D).

Prior efforts to genetically engineer mouse models of ELANE mutant congenital neutropenia failed to recapitulate a neutrophil maturation arrest phenotype (Grenda et al., 2002; Nanua et al., 2011), perhaps due to differences in the cellular stress associated with mutant ELANE during human versus mouse neutrophil development. We investigated if edited human HSPCs could reproduce the disease phenotype in immunodeficient mice. Human HSPCs were edited with sgRNAs targeting neutral locus, ELANE e2-C71 or ELANE e5-R220. Then the edited HSPCs were infused into immunodeficient NBSGW mice (McIntosh et al., 2015). Human engraftment and lineage contribution were assessed in the mouse bone marrow after 16 weeks (Fig. 5A). Overall human chimerism was similar among the three groups (Fig. S6A). Compared with normal myeloid development in the control group, the ELANE e5-R220 targeted group showed a defect in neutrophil maturation. Morphologic review of human myeloid cells demonstrated a paucity of band and segmented neutrophils with arrest at the promyelocyte/myelocyte stage (from 62.4% to 13.3%, p < 0.001, Fig. 5B–C). Immunophenotype analysis demonstrated a 96.4% reduction in CD16+ neutrophils (Fig. 5D). Patients with SCN typically demonstrate eosinophilia and monocytosis. Among residual human myeloid cells in the bone marrow, there was an increased relative contribution of promyelocytes (from 8.9% to 20.8%, p = 0.02), eosinophils (from 2.5% to 35.0%, p < 0.001) and monocytes (from 8.9% to 16.5%, p = 0.01) within the ELANE e5-R220 targeted group based on manual differential. Immunophenotype showed increase in the CD33+SSClow monocyte-enriched population (p = 0.008, Fig. S6A). Other lineages were similar between the ELANE e5-R220 targeted and control groups. The expression of UPR pathway genes BIP and ATF6 was increased in promyelocytes from the ELANE e5-R220 edited recipients (Fig. S6E–F). Gene edits were 92% in the input HSPC cell product for ELANE e5-R220 and remained 89–94% in engrafting HSPCs, lymphoid and erythroid cells, although reduced to 46% in the residual neutrophils (Fig. 3E). In contrast to e5-R220 editing, we observed no reduction in mature neutrophils based on immunophenotype or morphology with e2-C71 editing. Highly efficient gene edits were similarly distributed across all engrafting lineages, including 87–90% in HSPCs, lymphocytes, erythroid cells, monocytes, and neutrophils (Fig. S6B–C). ELANE e5-R220 edited hematopoietic cells were similarly competent for secondary transplantation as controls (Fig. S6D). ELANE e2-C71 editing showed similar primary and secondary human hematopoietic repopulation as the control group (Fig. 5D, S6A and S6D).

Despite the pronounced reduction in neutrophil maturation in the ELANE e5-R220 edited SCN xenograft model, we observed a few escaping neutrophils. Deep sequence analysis from these cells showed that unedited alleles were highly enriched (OR = 5.35, P < 0.001) and −1 frame indels were depleted (OR = 0.019, P < 0.001) as expected (Fig. 6A, S6G, Table S2). Unexpectedly, −2 frame indels were also enriched in, rather than depleted from, escaping neutrophils (OR = 14.68, P < 0.001). We sorted HSPC, promyelocyte, myelocyte, and neutrophil enriched populations from neutrophil maturation cultures following editing with ELANE e5-R220. Similar to the findings in the xenograft, we found −1 frame indels depleted and −2 frame indels enriched in neutrophils (Fig. 6B, Table S3). We analyzed the data from targeted amplicon sequencing of ELANE in bulk neutrophil maturation cultures edited by 9 different late exon targeting RNPs to compare indel frequencies with abundance of neutrophils and precursors. We found an inverse correlation between −1 frame indel frequency and neutrophil abundance (R = −0.693, P <0.001) (Fig. 6C). There was positive correlation between −2 frame indel frequency (R = 0.620, P < 0.001) and neutrophil abundance, and no significant correlation between inframe or unedited allele frequency and neutrophil abundance (Fig. 6D–F). The −1 frame indel frequency was also inversely correlated to myelocyte number but not to promyelocyte or HSPC number, suggesting that the selective loss of cells bearing −1 frame alleles occurs around the promyelocyte-to-myelocyte transition (Fig. S7A).

We reviewed the 23 frameshift mutations in ELANE that have been associated with congenital neutropenia (Germeshausen et al., 2013; Kim et al., 2015). Consistent with the selective impact of the gene edited alleles on neutrophil maturation, we found that all 23 disease-causing frameshift mutations result in a −1 frameshift, with indel lengths ranging from −7 to +8 bp (Fig. 7A, Table S4). None of these disease-associated indel mutations result in a −2 frame or inframe indel. Each of these disease-causing mutations leads to one of three possible PTCs (Fig. S7B–C). Distal −1 mutations that elude PTCs have also not been reported in patients with congenital neutropenia. These observations of human genetics were not previously appreciated to our knowledge but are consistent with our finding that late exon −2 frame gene edits do not elicit neutrophil maturation arrest.

To explore the mechanism why −2 frame is protective from neutrophil maturation arrest, we identified a guide RNA that generated predominantly −2 frame indels in ELANE exon 4, e4-V190 #1 (Fig. S7D, Table S2). Of all sgRNAs targeting ELANE late exons, this RNP had the least impact on neutrophil output (Fig. S3D). Unlike the early exon editing that resulted in mRNA decay, ELANE e4-V190 #1 editing was associated with preserved ELANE mRNA level (Fig. 7B). However, neutrophil elastase protein level was substantially reduced following ELANE e4-V190 #1 editing (Fig. 7C). ELANE late exon −2 frame indels lead to a C-terminal peptide extended by 19 AA with a shortened 3’UTR (17 nt vs 79 nt) (Fig. S7B–C). We speculated that the preserved mRNA level with reduced protein level could reflect inefficient translation. We performed polysome profiling with mRNA fractionation to measure ELANE mRNA levels in the actively translating polysome compared to translationally inactive fractions. We evaluated cell extracts after editing with neutral locus, ELANE e4-V190 #1 (74% −2 frame indels) and e5-R220 (78% −1 frame indels) sgRNAs (Fig. S7D). The overall polysome profile was similar in each of the three groups (Fig. 7D, S7E). We observed that ELANE e4-V190 #1 editing with −2 frame indels resulted in a shift of ELANE mRNA from polysome to monosome fractions, suggesting these mutations result in reduced translation (Fig. 7E–F, S7E). In contrast, neutral locus editing and ELANE e5-R220 editing gave similar results in terms of ELANE distribution between monosomes and polysomes. Given the preservation of overall transcript length following −2 frame editing, we reasoned that the reduced translation efficiency might be due to the frameshifted C-terminal extension or short 3’UTR. To investigate these possibilities, we cloned and expressed either the wt 3’UTR or −2 frame 3’UTR immediately following either ELANE wt or −2 frame amino-terminally epitope-tagged coding sequence (4 different constructs) and analyzed mRNA and protein level (Fig. S7F). Each of the 4 constructs yielded similar mRNA level (Fig. S7G). Both ELANE wt and −2 frame coding sequence constructs showed reduced protein expression when followed by −2 frame 3’UTR as compared to wt 3’UTR (Fig. S7H). These results suggest that the short −2 frame 3’UTR is sufficient to reduce protein production as compared to the full-length wt 3’UTR. The translational repression of mRNAs containing −2 frame indels is consistent with our earlier observations that reducing the neutrophil elastase gene product prevents neutrophil maturation arrest.

This study emphasizes several advantages of gene editing primary human cells to investigate disease genetics, pathophysiology and therapy. First, most prior efforts at collecting multiplexed functional data to correlate human genetic variation with clinically relevant experimental phenotypes have focused on simple cellular phenotypes evaluable in transformed cell lines (Findlay et al., 2018; Gelman et al., 2019). In this report we demonstrated the feasibility to conduct a gene-focused Cas9 dense mutagenesis screen in primary human HSPCs to identify ELANE variants associated with neutrophil maturation defects. We developed a dual delivery protocol with pooled sgRNA lentivirus transduction and SpCas9 expressing temperature-sensitive Sendai virus transient infection. In primary hematopoietic cells we faithfully recapitulated known genetic features such as the restriction of pathogenic frameshift mutations to terminal ELANE exons. We substantiated NMD as a key determinant of ELANE variant pathogenicity. Moreover, we identified genotype-phenotype features that have eluded prior recognition. Only −1 frame ELANE frameshifts that produce PTCs elicit neutrophil maturation arrest in our experimental model as well as in congenital neutropenia patients. In contrast, late exon −2 frame indels produce translational repression, revealing an unappreciated layer of ELANE gene regulation and a possible strategy to supersede dominant acting alleles. We found that the short 3’UTR associated with late exon −2 frame indels is associated with reduced protein production and speculate this may be due to impaired RNA binding protein interactions, although the molecular mechanism requires future study. We note a related example for late exon FBN1 indels associated with Marfanoid-progeroid-lipodystrophy syndrome (MPLS) in which all 5 unique MPLS-associated indels result in −2 frame (Lin et al., 2020), suggesting that selective pathogenicity based on indel frame of frameshifted transcripts that escape NMD may represent a more general genetic phenomenon.

Second, this work highlights how xenografts of gene-edited human HSCs can produce an animal model of ELANE mutant SCN not possible with conventional mouse genetic engineering. Prior efforts to recreate SCN through mouse modeling human ELANE mutations failed to elicit neutropenia, as mouse neutrophil precursors do not succumb to pronounced cell death upon expression of aberrant neutrophil elastase. Here we used a human hematopoietic xenograft system to produce an animal model of ELANE mutant SCN including characteristic neutrophil maturation arrest at the promyelocyte-to-myelocyte stage. This animal model offers opportunities to study the pathogenesis of SCN and investigate novel therapeutic interventions.

Third, highly efficient gene editing of human hematopoietic stem cells could itself serve as a therapy to produce a gene-modified cell product for autologous transplantation (Wu et al., 2019). Although in principle templated homology-directed repair can directly correct disease-associated mutations, challenges include the requirement for additional delivery of extrachromosomal DNA template, need for bespoke correction strategies for sundry patient-specific mutations, concurrent nonhomologous repair, and relative inefficiency in quiescent HSCs. Nonhomologous end joining is a simpler and more efficient DNA repair pathway to harness if a suitable therapeutic target for gene disruption may be identified. Dominant mutations of ELANE cause SCN whereas loss of neutrophil elastase has not been associated with SCN. Although neutrophil elastase is a major serine protease, neutrophils have other serine proteases such as proteinase 3 and cathepsin G that might partially replace its function (Kettritz, 2016), and moreover neutrophils possess multiple protease-independent mechanisms of microbial killing, including NADPH oxidase activity and release of cytoplasmic granule components including myeloperoxidase, lysozyme, and antimicrobial peptides. Papillon-Lefevre syndrome provides a model for the dispensability of neutrophil elastase in human host defense. This hereditary disorder results from loss of cathepsin C (dipeptidyl peptidase I, DPPI, CTSC) which is responsible for processing of the four major neutrophil granule serine proteases: neutrophil elastase, cathepsin G, proteinase 3, and neutrophil serine protease 4 (Pham et al., 2004; Sørensen et al., 2014). Papillon-Lefevre syndrome patients, deficient in all four neutrophil proteases, have only periodontitis and lack systemic immunodeficiency, neutropenia, or elevated MDS/AML risk. The mild phenotype of combined neutrophil serine protease deficiency suggests that isolated deficiency of neutrophil elastase would be unlikely to result in clinically significant infectious risk. Since neutrophil elastase appears dispensable, targeting indels to ELANE to trigger NMD could be a simple and universal approach to therapeutic gene editing for ELANE-mutant SCN. A recent study demonstrated that introducing indels to ELANE exon 2 could rescue neutrophil maturation from ELANE mutant cells in vitro (Nasri et al., 2020). Furthermore, this study showed that ELANE deficient neutrophils retain phagocytic, oxidative and chemotactic functions. In our report, we demonstrate substantially higher efficiency of gene editing in HSPCs (including from SCN patients) to achieve essentially quantitative therapeutic gene edits; characterize induction of nonsense mediated decay (NMD) as the critical therapeutic molecular action; describe dozens of suitable therapeutic target sequences at ELANE through pooled screening; and apply a unique animal model to show that therapeutic editing of ELANE is not only feasible but highly efficient in bona fide human HSCs that retain normal neutrophil maturation potential in vivo and self-renewal capacity shown by primary and secondary engraftment.

Prior studies have shown that some ELANE mutations affecting the canonical translation initiation site or activating a downstream IRES lead to production of amino-terminally truncated isoforms (Tidwell et al., 2014). Here we found that introducing indels in ELANE exon 2 induces NMD and does not result in detectable re-initiated amino-terminally truncated NE isoforms; however the potential for NMD induction or translation re-initiation should be carefully considered as various ELANE gene edits are considered in the context of heterogenous ELANE mutations.

Following autologous engraftment of ELANE gene edited HSPCs, there would be anticipated heterogeneous allelic outcomes. Some cells would be unedited while other cells would have only the normal allele edited, still both conditions would lead to neutrophil maturation arrest. Most of the cells would have either the mutant allele edited or both the mutant and normal alleles edited, which would restore neutrophil maturation with or without neutrophil elastase, and likely relieve chronic myeloid stress and requirement for G-CSF therapy, thus mitigating MDS/AML risk. Human ELANE mosaicism indicates that even a fraction, as low as 11%, of hematopoietic precursors with neutrophil maturation potential prevents neutropenia and MDS/AML development (Ancliff et al., 2002; Hirata et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019; Malcov et al., 2010; Newburger et al., 2010).

In summary, pooled CRISPR screening of ELANE in human HSPCs recapitulated disease-associated pathogenic variants, uncovered a translational layer of gene regulation, established an SCN animal model, and identified numerous promising target sequences for universal therapeutic gene editing.

### Limitations of the Study

This study uses SpCas9 nuclease to introduce indel mutations to ELANE to investigate congenital neutropenia. A limitation is that SpCas9 nuclease cannot directly install missense mutations. Future studies using other genome editing methods like base editing could analyze other classes of mutations. Our studies suggest that frame −2 mutations in late exons of ELANE result in translational repression due to presence of a short 3’UTR sequence, however the molecular mechanisms whereby the 3’UTR controls translational efficiency will require future investigation. We used the NBSGW xenograft model to study the function of gene edited human hematopoietic cells in a bone marrow environment. Limitations of this model include that it lacks human stroma and does not produce robust peripheral blood engraftment of human neutrophils.

### EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND SUBJECT DETAILS

#### Normal hematopoietic cell samples and cell culture

Human CD34+ HSPCs from mobilized peripheral blood of deidentified healthy donors were purchased from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Research Center, Seattle, Washington. Congenital neutropenia patient bone marrow samples were collected following Boston Children’s Hospital institutional review board (IRB) approval and informed patient consent. CD34+ HSPCs were cultured in StemSpan SFEM medium (StemCell Technologies, Vancouver, Canada) supplemented with 1x StemSpan CD34+ expansion supplement (Cat# 02691, STEMCELL Technology).

#### Mice and Animal Housing

All animal experiments were approved by the Boston Children’s Hospital Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. Non-irradiated NOD.Cg-KitW−41JTyr+PrkdcscidIl2rgtm1Wjl (NBSGW) female mice 4–5 weeks of age (Jackson Laboratory, Bar Harbor, Maine) were infused by retro-orbital injection with 1M edited human CD34+ HSPCs (resuspended in 200 μl PBS).

### METHOD DETAILS

#### ELANE dense mutagenesis library design and cloning

All NGG protospacer adjacent motif (PAM) restricted sgRNAs targeting cleavages to ELANE coding sequence at least 2 bp away from exon junctions (n = 186) plus sgRNAs targeting both positive control genes (n = 44) and neutral loci (n = 100) were synthesized by oligonucleotide array and cloned as pool to lentivirus (Supplementary Table 2). The negative control sgRNAs target genomic regions without annotated function (Morgens et al., 2017). The positive control genes included all 11 genes besides ELANE associated with terms “severe congenital neutropenia” or “Shwachman-Diamond syndrome” in OMIM (CSF3R, EFL1, G6PC3, GFI1, HAX1, JAGN1, SBDS, SRP54, VPS45, WAS) as well as CEBPA, a known critical transcription factor for neutrophil development (Zhang et al., 1997). The sgRNA sequences targeting positive control genes were selected from the Brunello genome-wide library (Doench et al., 2016). The lentiviral sgRNA library was constructed as previously described (Canver et al., 2015; Shalem et al., 2014; Sher et al., 2019). Briefly, the sgRNA oligos were synthesized and amplified using PCR. A second PCR was performed to remove barcodes and insert vector homology. Subsequently, oligos were cloned into LentiGuide-Puro (Addgene plasmid 52963) using Gibson assembly (Doench et al., 2016). Representation of the sgRNAs within the library was verified by next-generation sequencing (NGS).

#### Cell culture and lentivirus packaging

HEK293T cells (ATCC, cat# CRL-3216) and HL-60 cells (from P.E.N.) were cultured with DMEM and RPMI-1640 Medium, separately. To make the complete growth medium, fetal bovine serum (FBS) was added to a final concentration of 10%. To produce lentivirus, HEK293T cells were transfected at 70–80% confluence with 13.3 μg pf psPAX2, 6.7 μg VSV-G and 20 μg of the lentiviral construct plasmid of interest using 180 μg of linear polyethylenimine in 15 cm tissue culture dishes. Lentiviral supernatant was collected at both 48 h and 72 h post-transfection and concentrated by ultracentrifugation at 24,000 rpm for 4 h at 4 °C with a Beckman Coulter SW 32 Ti rotor.

#### Reverse genetic plasmid and rescue of temperature-sensitive recombinant Sendai virus (rSeV)

The basis for ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9 (manuscript in preparation) was our recombinant Sendai virus with an eGFP reporter inserted between the N and P genes via duplication of the N-to-P intergenic region, derived from RGV0 (kind gift of Nancy McQueen), a Fushimi strain SeV with mutations in the F and M genes that allow trypsin-independent growth(Hou et al., 2005). FLAG-tagged codon-optimized SpCas9 was amplified from pX330 (Cong et al., 2013) (Addgene, cat#42230) and inserted into rSeV following the eGFP reporter, linked with a P2A ribosomal skipping sequence (ATNFSLLKQAGDVEENPGP). The P2A sequence was preceded by a GSG linker to ensure complete ribosomal skipping. A total of 6 additional mutations were introduced across the Sendai virus P (D433A, R434A, K437A, L511F) and L (L15581I K1795E) genes, which together confer temperature-restriction of the virus. This combination of mutations was selected following characterization of combinations of these and other mutations, drawing on previous work (Ban et al., 2011). Characterization of the novel ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9 demonstrated that while infection was highly efficient at 32–34°C, no infection was detectable by eGFP expression at 37°C, even at multiplicities of infection that achieved close to 100% infection at the permissive temperatures. Following initial infection at 32–34°C, shifting infected cells to 37°C blocked ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9 replication and gene expression, with no detectable viral titer in cell supernatants, and gradual loss of virally-expressed proteins. Details of the reverse genetic plasmid of ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9 was demonstrated in our previous study (Park et al., 2016). Rescue of replication-competent Sendai virus from transfected plasmid was performed as follows. BSR-T7 cells cultured at 32°C in six-well plates were transfected with 4 μg T7-driven antigenome, 1.44 μg T7-N, 0.77 μg T7-P, 0.07 μg T7-L, and 4 μg codon-optimized T7 polymerase, using Lipofectamine LTX (Invitrogen). Virus rescue was monitored by appearance and spread of eGFP fluorescence, and rescued virus was further expanded on BSR-T7 cells. Virus titers were determined by titration on Vero CCL-81 cells at 32°C for 48 h, with individual infection events counted by eGFP fluorescence at 48 h post-infection in a Celigo plate reader (TTP Labtech, Melbourn, UK).

#### Neutrophil maturation culture of human CD34+ HSPCs

To induce neutrophil differentiation from CD34+ HSPCs, the cytokine cocktail of G-CSF 3 ng/mL (unless concentration otherwise indicated), IL-3 5 ng/mL, FLT3-Ligand 100 ng/mL, and SCF 50 ng/ml was supplemented to the culture media for 10 days (+/−1 day) before analysis, with GM-CSF 5 ng/ml included in the culture media for the first 4 days. All cytokines of human origin and from PeproTech (Rocky Hill, NJ).

#### Pooled CRISPR/SpCas9 screening and analysis

CD34+ HSPCs were transduced with the corresponding sgRNA-library lentivirus pool at low multiplicity of infection (Fig. S1H). CD34+ HSPCs were transiently infected with ts-rSev-eGFP-SpCas9 at high multiplicity of infection 12 h later, to ensure at least 95% infection efficiency (Fig. S1) and maintained at 34 °C for 2 days. Subsequently, 1 μg/mL puromycin (Sigma) were added to select for lentiviral library integrants in cells. After 10-day differentiation, cells were washed with PBS and stained with anti-human antibody for CD34 conjugated with PE-Cy7 (581), CD117 with APC (104D2) and CD16 with PE (3G8) and sorted for CD34−CD117+CD16− and CD34−CD117−CD16+ populations. Library preparation and deep sequencing was performed as previously described (Shalem et al., 2014). Briefly, genomic DNA was extracted using Qiagen Blood and Tissue kit. Herculase PCR reaction using LentiGuide-Puro specific primers was performed to generate the library for Illumina MiSeq paired-end sequencing. Guide sequences present in each pool were enumerated. Enrichment for each sgRNA was determined as the log2 transformation of the median number of occurrences of a particular sgRNA in CD34−CD117+CD16− promyelocyte population divided by the median number of occurrences of the same sgRNA in the CD34− CD117−CD16+ neutrophil population. With DESeq2, a Wald test statistic was computed along with a probability (P-value) for each sgRNA to test the difference in read counts between the CD34− CD117+CD16− promyelocyte and CD34−CD117−CD16+ neutrophil populations. sgRNAs were then mapped to the transcript sequence by mapping the predicted double strand break site to the codons nearest the double strand break. sgRNA spacer sequences with GC ≤30% or ≥80% were excluded from further analysis given inferior efficiency (Doench et al., 2014b; Wang et al., 2014). LOESS regression, one method for local polynomial regression, was performed to reveal the trend of enrichment score for sgRNAs targeting different ELANE codons, using known sgRNA enrichment scores and locations as input. 95% confidence intervals were generated with these regressions.

#### Preparation of 3xNLS-SpCas9 and RNP electroporation

For SpCas9 protein expression, RIPL-BL21 (DE3)-competent cells transformed with 3xNLS-Cas9 (Wu et al., 2019) plasmid (Addgene #114365) were grown in terrific broth TB media at 37 °C and switched to 18 °C until OD600 reached 1.6–1.8. Cells were induced by 1 mM isopropyl ß-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside with 10 mM MgCl2 for 16–20 h. For protein purification, cell paste was collected and lysed in PBS buffer containing 500 mM NaCl and 10% glycerol with EDTA free protease inhibitor tablet (SigmaAldrich S8830) using microfluidizer (20000 Psi). The lysate was centrifuged at 18,000g for 40 min. Proteins were purified using nickel affinity (Buffer A: 50 mM Tris pH8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol; Buffer B: 50 mM Tris pH8.0, 500 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol, 250 mM imidazole), cation exchange (Buffer A: 20 mM HEPES pH7.3; 10% glycerol; Buffer B: 20 mM HEPES pH7.3, 1 M NaCl, 10% glycerol), and Superdex 200 size exclusion columns (20 mM HEPES pH7.3, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol) sequentially. The purified protein was concentrated in 20 mM HEPES pH7.3, 150 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol buffer. The purity and quality of protein fractions were examined by separation using SDS-PAGE gel and then staining using GelCode Blue Stain Reagent (Fisher). The chemically modified sgRNA (2′-O-methyl-3′-phosphorothioate modifications in the first and last three nucleotides) was synthesized (Synthego). sgRNA concentration is calculated by the OD reporting method. CD34+ HSPCs were thawed and cultured in StemSpan SFEM (STEMCELL Technology) with 1x StemSpan CD34+ expansion supplement (Cat# 02691, STEMCELL Technology) for 24 h. Electroporation was performed using Lonza 4D Nucleofector (V4XP-3032 for 20 μl Nucleocuvette Strips or V4XP-3024 for 100 μl Nucleocuvettes) following the manufacturer’s instructions. For 20 μl Nucleocuvette Strips, the RNP complex was prepared by mixing 3xNLS-SpCas9 (100 pmol) and sgRNA (300 pmol) and incubating for 15 min at room temperature immediately before electroporation. 30% glycerol solution was added to Cas9 protein prior to addition of sgRNA for a final concentration of 2% glycerol. 50K HSPCs resuspended in 20 μl P3 solution were mixed with RNP and transferred to a cuvette for electroporation with program EO-100. For 100 μl cuvette electroporation, the RNP complex was made by mixing 500 pmol Cas9 and 1500 pmol sgRNA. 5M HSPCs were resuspended in 100 μl P3 solution for RNP electroporation as described above. The electroporated cells were cultured in StemSpan SFEM with 1x StemSpan CD34+ expansion supplement before induced differentiation. Guide RNA spacer sequences listed in Supplementary Table 3.

#### Indel frequency analysis

Indel frequencies were measured with bulk cell cultures 5 days after electroporation. Briefly, genomic DNA was extracted using the Qiagen Blood and Tissue kit. Genomic region surrounding the sgRNA targeting site was amplified using either AccuPrime GC-Rich DNA polymerase (ThermoFisher Scientific, Cat# 12337016) for sgRNA ELANE e2–71C targeting site or HotStarTaq DNA polymerase (QIAGEN, Cat# 203203) for other PCR reactions strictly following the manufactory instructions with variable annealing temperature. PCR products were subject to Sanger sequencing and then TIDE analysis to identifies the major induced mutations within 30 bp away from the projected editing site and accurately determines their frequency in a cell population(Brinkman et al., 2014). For amplicon deep sequencing, we generated amplicon libraries with 2 rounds of PCR using primers containing sample-specific barcodes and adapter. Amplicons were then sequenced for 2 × 150 bp paried-end reads with MiniSeq Sequencing system (Illumina). The deep sequencing data were analyzed by CRISPResso (Clement et al., 2019) software with the following parameters: a minimum alignment identity of 75%, window size of 2 bp around the cleavage site to quantify indels, an average PHRED quality score of 30, and excluded substitutions to limit potential false-positives.

#### Cell counting, flow cytometry analysis and apoptosis detection

Cell counting was performed using either CountBright Absolute Counting Beads, for flow cytometry (ThermoFisher Scientific, Cat# C36950) or hemocytometer. For analysis of surface markers, cells were stained in PBS containing 2% (w/v) BSA, with anti-human CD45 (HI30), anti-human CD34 (581), anti-human CD33 (P67.6), anti-human CD117 (104D2), anti-human CD16 (3G8), anti-human CD14 (63D3), anti-human CD235a (HI264), anti-human CD3 (UCHT1), anti-human CD19 (HIB19) and anti-mouse CD45 (30-F11). GFP positive cells after ts-rSeV-eGFP-SpCas9 transient infection were determined using flow cytometry. For apoptosis analysis, the Annexin V-APC staining kit was used according to the manufacturer’s instructions (550474, BD PharMingen). Flow cytometry data were acquired on a LSRII or LSR Fortessa (BD Biosciences) and analyzed using FlowJo software (Tree Star).

#### Determination of ELANE mRNA and protein level

Total RNA was extracted from cell cultures 4 days after induced differentiation in vitro (unless indicated elsewhere) using the RNeasy Plus Mini Kit (QIAGEN), and reverse transcribed using the iScript cDNA synthesis kit (Biorad) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. ELANE mRNA was quantified using real-time Q-PCR with GAPDH as an internal control. For quantification of ELANE protein level, whole cell lysates were collected after 10-day neutrophil maturation culture which were then subject to ELISA analysis using the PMN (neutrophil) elastase human ELISA kit (ThermoFisher) strictly following the manufacturer’s instructions. All gene expression data represent the mean of at least three biological replicates.

#### Immunophenotyping of human CD34+ HSPCs xenograft from NBSGW mice

Bone marrow was isolated for human xenograft analysis 16 weeks after human CD34+ HSPCs engraftment. Half the bone marrow was used for secondary transplantation and the other half for analyses. For flow cytometry analysis, bone marrow cells were first incubated with Human TruStainFcX (422302, BioLegend) and TruStainfcX (anti-mouse CD16/32, 101320, BioLegend) blocking antibodies for 10 min and then stained with marker panels designed for multi-lineage analysis, including anti-mouse CD45 (30-F11), anti-human CD45 (HI30), anti-human CD34 (581), anti-human CD33 (P67.6), anti-human CD117 (104D2), anti-human CD16 (3G8), anti-human CD14 (63D3), anti-human CD235a (HI264), anti-human CD3 (UCHT1), anti-human CD19 (HIB19), and Fixable Viability Dye eFluor 780 for live/dead staining (65-0865-14, Thermo Fisher). Percentage human engraftment was calculated as hCD45+ cells/(hCD45+ + mCD45+ cells). Cell sorting was performed on a FACSAria II machine (BD Biosciences).

#### Polysome profiling

CD34+ HSPCs were edited by RNP electroporation and then subject to neutrophil maturation culture for 7 days. Then total cells were incubated with 100 mg/ml of cycloheximide (Sigma Aldrich) for 5 min at 37 °C, washed twice with ice-cold PBS containing 100 mg/ml of cycloheximide and lysed in 10 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 5 mM MgCl2, 100mM KCl, 1% Triton X-100, 3 mM DTT, 100 mg/ml cycloheximide, 500 U/ml RNasin (Promega) and 1x Complete Protease Inhibitor, EDTA-free (Roche) as well as 1x Protease Inhibitor Set (without EDTA) (G-Biosciences). Polysomes were separated on a 5%–50% linear sucrose gradient containing 20 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 5 mM MgCl2, 100 mM KCl, 3 mM DTT, 100 mg/ml cycloheximide and 20 U/ml SUPERase, In RNase Inhibitor (Ambion) and centrifuged at 45,000 g for 1 h 15 min in a SW41 rotor in an L8–80M ultracentrifuge (Beckman Coulter). Equal amounts of in vitro transcribed firefly luciferase mRNA were added to fraction as a normalization control. Total RNA from each fraction was purified using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) and reverse transcription was performed with the iScript cDNA synthesis kit (Biorad). ELANE mRNA level was determined by real-time qPCR.

#### Rapid amplification of 3’ cDNA end (3’ RACE) analysis

3’ RACE was performed with a forward primer annealing to ELANE coding sequence and the reverse primer annealing to polyA sequence (Supplementary Table 4). PCR products were further cloned into pLVX-Puro vector (Clontech) and Sanger sequencing was performed.

#### Western blots

Cells were lysed in 2x Laemmli sample buffer (Bio-Rad, 1610737) and total cellular lysates were then subjected to SDS-PAGE followed by transfer to PVDF membrane. Detection of FLAG-NE and NE was done using anti-FLAG (Sigma, F1804; 1:1000) and anti-NE antibody (s generous gift from Marshall S. Horwitz; 1:1000), and HRP-conjugated secondary antibody, followed by Pierce™ ECL Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Scientific, Cat# 32106). Cofilin was used as internal control.

### QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS

All statistical analyses were performed with R package and GraphPad Prism 8. All pairwise comparisons were assessed using unpaired two-tailed Student’s t test unless otherwise indicated in the main text or in the figure legends. Correlation between two groups was assessed by either Pearson correlation or Spearman correlation as indicated in the figure legends. Pearson’s chi-squared test was applied to compare allelic distribution between different cell populations. Results were considered significant if the P value was < 0.05.

## In Brief

Discovery of genes driving axolotl limb regeneration has been challenging, due to limited genomic resources. Bryant et al. have created a transcriptome with near-complete sequence information for most axolotl genes, identiﬁed transcriptional proﬁles that distinguish blastemas from differentiated limb tissues, and uncovered functional roles for cirbp and kazald1 in limb regeneration.

## SUMMARY

Mammals have extremely limited regenerative capabilities; however, axolotls are profoundly regenerative and can replace entire limbs. The mechanisms underlying limb regeneration remain poorly understood, partly because the enormous and incompletely sequenced genomes of axolotls have hindered the study of genes facilitating regeneration. We assembled and annotated a de novo transcriptome using RNA-sequencing proﬁles for a broad spectrum of tissues that is estimated to have nearcomplete sequence information for 88% of axolotl genes. We devised expression analyses that identi- ﬁed the axolotl orthologs of cirbp and kazald1 as highly expressed and enriched in blastemas. Using morpholino anti-sense oligonucleotides, we ﬁnd evidence that cirbp plays a cytoprotective role during limb regeneration whereas manipulation of kazald1 expression disrupts regeneration. Our transcriptome and annotation resources greatly complement previous transcriptomic studies and will be a valuable resource for future research in regenerative biology.

## INTRODUCTION

The limited capacity of humans to regenerate many tissues, organs, and appendages is a formidable clinical hurdle (Ziegler-Graham et al., 2008). Conversely, some animals, including invertebrates such as planaria and vertebrates such as amphibians, have remarkable regenerative capacity. Among those, many salamanders, including axolotls, can regenerate entire limbs throughout life (reviewed in Whited and Tabin, 2009). Elucidating the molecular mechanisms that enable such profound

regenerative capacity may provide key insights relevant to human regenerative medicine. The axolotl community has made signiﬁcant strides in advancing our understanding of limb regeneration, but our knowledge of the molecular mechanisms that underlie axolotl regeneration is still very limited. Unbiased genomics and transcriptomics can often unlock the molecular components of systems that have not been genetically tractable. Unfortunately, the axolotl genome remains mostly unsequenced and poses major challenges at 32 Gb in size (Keinath et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2009; Straus, 1971). RNA sequencing followed by de novo transcriptome assembly (Haas et al., 2013; Robertson et al., 2010; Schulz et al., 2012) has offered investigators an alternative for identifying near-full-length transcripts and performing differential gene expression analyses without genome mapping. Recent axolotl transcriptome studies (Knapp et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014; McCusker et al., 2015; Monaghan et al., 2009; Stewart et al., 2013; Voss et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2013) have focused on and signiﬁcantly advanced our understanding of the changes in transcription over time in the regenerating portion of the limb. However, an important missing component of the existing datasets is deep transcriptional information about each of the presumed parent tissue types within the limb, which contribute progenitors and serve as the template for the future regenerate limb. Thus, examining the transcripts that deﬁne them in the differentiated, homeostatic state will be critical for future comparisons with progenitor cells along the temporal path of regeneration. Here we combined RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) of diverse tissues with de novo transcriptome assembly, computational analysis, and experimental validation to develop a systematic map of the axolotl transcriptome. This assembly facilitated identiﬁcation of speciﬁc transcripts and classes of genes whose expression is associated with successful limb regeneration. We experimentally validated our transcriptome’s accuracy by analyzing mRNA expression of identiﬁed transcripts using in situ hybridization. Furthermore, we experimentally modiﬁed the expression of cirbp

## RESULTS

An RNA-Seq Catalog for Limb Tissues and Regeneration To build a reference map of axolotl limb regeneration, we proﬁled 42 samples across 16 different tissues (Figure 1A). First, we pro- ﬁled intact, unamputated limbs to reﬂect the starting—and end— point for limb regeneration. We sampled four positions along the proximal (shoulder) to distal (ﬁngertip) axis to identify any location-speciﬁc transcriptional differences. Second, we sequenced the blastema, a bud-like outgrowth at the tip of the regenerating limb that contains activated progenitor cells that regenerate the internal structures of the limb. To identify transcripts whose regulation distinguishes blastema cells, we removed the regenerate epithelium of blastemas at the medium-bud stage before it began to differentiate into the various tissues of the regenerating limb. Third, it is thought that axolotls are able to redeploy transcriptional programs that guide embryogenesis during limb regeneration, and a recent study demonstrated that genes with roles in germline cell renewal are required for axolotl limb regeneration (Zhu et al., 2012). To facilitate the systematic identiﬁcation of germline and embryonic transcriptional programs that are reactivated during regeneration, we generated transcriptional proﬁles for testes, ovaries, and embryos (one-cell to prehatch stage). Fourth, following amputation, individual tissues within the limb, including skeletal muscle, cartilage, bone, and blood vessels, may contribute activated progenitor cells to the regenerating limb (Kragl et al., 2009; Muneoka et al., 1986; Sandoval-Guzma´ n et al., 2014); reviewed in Knapp and Tanaka, 2012). We therefore sampled and analyzed each of these tissues to deﬁne tissue-speciﬁc expression and marker transcripts for the differentiated tissue types in limbs. We also included transcripts from heart and gill ﬁlaments in our assembly to increase the comprehensiveness of the transcriptome and to provide resources for researchers interested in pursuing questions outside of limb regeneration. Fifth, the blastema is an autonomous unit, programmed from the onset with spatial coordinates that instruct the regrowth of precisely the portion of the limb that has been lost (Crawford and Stocum, 1988a, 1988b; Echeverri and Tanaka, 2005; McCusker and Gardiner, 2013; Mercader et al., 2005; Stocum and Melton, 1977), such that amputation of the hand (a ‘‘distal’’ amputation) results in regeneration of a hand, but amputation of an entire arm (a ‘‘proximal’’ amputation)

results in regeneration of an arm. To assess how information is differentially encoded in proximal versus distal blastemas, we sequenced medium-bud-stage blastemas derived from both proximal and distal amputations.

A De Novo Assembled Axolotl Transcriptome We assembled 42 RNA-seq samples totaling 1.3 billion 100- base paired-end reads (Table S1) using Trinity (Grabherr et al., 2011; Haas et al., 2013). We ﬁrst combined reads from all samples and performed in silico normalization, retaining 6.6% of reads for assembly (86 million paired-end reads). We then used Trinity (Table S1) to generate an assembly of 1,554,055 transcript contigs clustered into 1,388,798 ‘‘gene’’ groupings (Data S1 and S2; median transcript length: 288 bases, N50 of 606 bases). Although our in silico normalization ﬁltered out the vast majority of the reads prior to assembly, 80% of the original reads mapped back to the assembly, with most mapping as properly paired reads (Figure S1A). The majority of the transcriptome corresponds to lowly expressed transcript contigs (Figure 1B), as 90% of the total transcription is represented by an ‘‘E90 transcript set’’ of 26,378 transcripts (20,506 genes, E90- N50 of 3,511) (Table S1; Figure 1C).

Functional Annotation with Trinotate and Assessment of Transcriptome Completeness Annotating de novo assembled transcripts in the absence of an assembled genome, as in the case of the axolotl, remains a bioinformatics challenge with few available tools. We therefore developed Trinotate (http://trinotate.github.io), an annotation protocol and toolkit for de novo assembled transcriptomes. Trinotate extracts predicted coding regions using TransDecoder (http://transdecoder.github.io), searches both the entire transcripts and the predicted coding regions separately for protein homology by BLAST search against Swiss-Prot, and annotates the coding regions for domain content, signal peptides, and transmembrane domains. Trinotate reports its annotations in a convenient tab-delimited ﬁle (Data S3). We applied Trinotate to the 1.6 million transcripts in our assembly, ﬁnding a large number of likely full-length transcripts enriched in the E90 set. Trinotate reported 109,180 transcripts matching 29,529 unique Swiss-Prot proteins, with 27,056 Trinity transcripts matching 13,501 proteins across at least 80% of the matching protein’s length. These transcripts likely represent fully or near-fully reconstructed transcripts with detectable homologs in other species, of which over a third (9,950) are signiﬁcantly enriched (22-fold; p value < 2.2 3 1016, Fisher’s exact test) among the E90 transcript set. By subjecting our transcriptome to BUSCO analysis (Sim~ao et al., 2015), we identiﬁed by this measure that our transcriptome

Differential Expression Analysis Identiﬁed Tissue- Speciﬁc Gene Expression and Splicing We estimated the expression proﬁles for all transcripts across all samples, and found excellent correlation between biological replicates (average Pearson correlation between replicates: 0.90; Figure 1D). As expected, samples derived from similar tissues (e.g., sections of the arm segments; bone and cartilage; proximal and distal blastemas) had more highly correlated expression than more distinct tissues such as the testes, which exhibited the most divergent transcriptional proﬁle. We next identiﬁed differentially expressed transcripts, conservatively focusing on transcripts identiﬁed as differentially expressed by multiple methods (Figure S1B) and restricted to samples with biological replicates (this excludes gill ﬁlament and embryos, which were used only for assembly). We identiﬁed 60,355 transcripts corresponding to 41,697 genes as at least 2-fold signiﬁcantly differentially expressed (FDR % 0.05) between at least two tissue-type comparisons (Data S4 and S5). Finally, we used a graph-based analysis to identify genes that are differentially expressed across each set of tissues (Figure 2A). In this approach, a graph is constructed for each differentially expressed transcript such that each tissue type is represented by a node, and an edge is drawn from a signiﬁcantly upregulated tissue node to the downregulated tissue node. The graph is then partitioned to identify the maximal set of upregulated tissues for that transcript. Visualization of the graphical output for a given transcript intuitively presents the tissue(s) with the highest expression level for the transcript of interest (Figure 2A). Of the differentially expressed transcripts, 14,594 transcripts (11,523 genes) were most tissue enriched given all pairwise tissue comparisons (Figure 2B; Table S2). Testes and ovaries had the most tissue-enriched transcripts (7,795

and 2,247, respectively, together 69%), followed by skeletal muscle tissue (961 transcripts) and the combination of all arm-segmented tissues (elbow, forearm, upper arm, and hand; 892) compared to each of the remaining tissues, including those tissues that compose the arm (e.g., bone). The tissue-speciﬁc transcripts were enriched for physiologically relevant functional categories based on enrichment analysis of Gene Ontology (GO) terms assigned from Swiss- Prot annotations of homologous proteins using Trinotate (e.g., spermatogenesis was enriched in testis-speciﬁc genes [FDR < 5.5e44], muscle contraction for skeletal muscle [FDR < 5.1e20], etc.; Table S2). We experimentally validated by in situ hybridization and RT-PCR some of the tissue-enriched expression predictions to demonstrate our ability to correctly predict diverse tissue-speciﬁc gene expression patterns (Figures 2C–2J). For example, as predicted by our analysis, speriolin (spermatogenesis and centriole associated 1; spatc1) is enriched in germ cells within the testes (Figure 2C). This is consistent with limited studies on Speriolin that demonstrate this protein associates with centrosomes in spermatocytes and exhibits testis-speciﬁc expression in mice (Goto and Eddy, 2004; Goto et al., 2010). Finally, we identiﬁed differentially expressed transcripts that are also associated with differential isoform usage across tissues. Of the 60,355 differentially expressed transcripts (41,697 genes), there are 29,750 transcripts (11,092 genes) with putative alternatively spliced isoforms. For 7,300 genes, the alternative isoforms have different patterns of tissue enrichment, suggestive of alternate functional roles (Table S3). Most of these genes (4,097 of 7,300) have at least one isoform signiﬁcantly enriched in either testes or ovaries, with far fewer genes with evidence for tissue-speciﬁc isoforms in other tissues (e.g., 96 genes involving alternate isoform enrichment between heart and skeletal muscle). Notably, only 346 genes of the 11,523 genes with strong tissue-speciﬁc expression (Figure 2B) show evidence for tissue-speciﬁc isoform usage, the vast majority (315 genes) in either testes or ovaries. A Transcriptional Program for Blastemas Implicates the RNA Life Cycle in Limb Regeneration We next analyzed the 159 transcripts (151 genes) differentially induced in all blastema samples (proximal and distal) as compared to all other sampled tissues (Figure 3A; Table S4). Notably, many of the blastema-speciﬁc genes (64/151) do not have a similar sequence identiﬁed in another organism in the UniRef90 database (E % 103; BLASTX). Nonetheless, several blastema-speciﬁc genes have known blastema relevance (e.g., twist family bhlh transcription factor 1 [twist1] [Satoh et al., 2008]) or are predicted to encode proteins in pathways implicated in salamander limb regeneration (retinol-binding protein 2a [rbp2a] [Maden, 1983]; matrix metallopeptidase 11 [mmp11] [Yang et al., 1999]). In particular, we identiﬁed the T box transcription factor tbx5, previously reported as enriched in forelimb blastemas (Khan et al., 2002), discriminating its tissue-speciﬁc expression among 13 total tbx genes detected in this axolotl transcriptome. Furthermore, when analyzing forelimb blastemas, our differential expression analysis did not erroneously uncover tbx4, which has been documented to only be upregulated in hindlimb blastemas (Khan et al., 2002). Several blastema-speciﬁc genes are predicted to encode RNA-binding proteins, highlighting a potential role for the regulation of the RNA life cycle in regeneration (Figure 3A, highlighted). Among the blastema-induced transcripts are three predicted heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnrnp) transcripts, an RNA-binding motif (rbm3) ortholog, a serine/arginine-rich RNA splicing factor (sfrs1) ortholog, and the axolotl ortholog of cold-inducible RNA-binding protein (cirbp). Interestingly, a newt ortholog of cirbp was recently identiﬁed in a subtractive hybridization screen as upregulated in limb blastemas compared to non-amputated limbs (Jiang et al., 2014), raising the possibility that cirbp and its homologs may be important regulators in regeneration across species. We also validated several of the blastema-enriched genes by in situ hybridization (Figure 3B), and conﬁrmed they are not appreciably expressed in unamputated limbs (Figure 3C). We further explored the expression of cirbp during limb regeneration and found that cirbp expression was apparent as early as 3 days post-amputation (Figure 4A), persisted as the blastema consolidates, and grows through palette formation (Figures 4B–4D). Past studies have demonstrated that CIRBP proteins regulate cell fate by inhibiting pro-apoptotic pathways during newt spermatogenesis (Eto et al., 2009) and in the mammalian nervous system (Zhang et al., 2015). To further explore an antiapoptotic role for axolotl cirbp in limb regeneration, we delivered

a translation-blocking morpholino to early blastemas (Figure S2) and assayed cell death using TUNEL staining 4 days later. Administration of cirbp-targeting morpholino caused a signiﬁ- cant increase in the percentage of TUNEL-positive blastema cells relative to PBS and standard morpholino controls (cirbptargeting morpholino: n = 19 limbs; standard control morpholino: n = 11 limbs; PBS control: n = 5 limbs) (Figures 4E–4G). These results suggest a conserved role for Cirbp-related proteins in regulating cell death across vertebrates and highlight a cytoprotective role for RNA-binding proteins within blastema cells. We also examined the 60 transcripts speciﬁcally downregulated in blastemas (Figure S3). These included transcripts that encode proteins that likely regulate fatty acid metabolism (prkab2, cyp2a13, and faah), glucose metabolism (pgm1 and gp1), the cell cycle (ccng1), and mitochondrial respiration (cox7a2 and cox7a2l). The expression of most of these blastema-repressed transcripts is higher in skeletal muscle than in bone and cartilage (e.g., casq1), suggesting that blastema cells may be more actively repressing a muscle program than a skeletal program.

Kazd1 is predicted to have a Kazal-type serine protease inhibitor domain, a follistatin-like domain, and an immunoglobulin domain. We found that kazald1 expression is not detectable in the intact limb pre-amputation, increases shortly after amputation, is maintained during the blastemal stages of regeneration, and is dramatically downregulated near the end of regeneration (Figures 5B and 5C). Motivated by the ﬁnding that kazald1 is essential for normal regeneration, we leveraged our transcriptome to create kazald1-targeted deletions in both embryos and unamputated limbs via electroporation (Supplemental Information; Figure S5) to further complement our studies with morpholino knockdown. Nevertheless, future studies with complete genetic loss of function of kazald1 are warranted and will prove highly valuable to further examining this gene’s mechanistic role in axolotl limb regeneration. kazald1’s intense expression within the transient blastema structure suggests that it has a time-delineated function during regeneration. To test this, we used a replication-incompetent retrovirus (Whited et al., 2013) to constitutively overexpress kazald1 in regenerating limbs (Figure S6A). A majority (15/22) of kazald1-infected limbs regenerated abnormally compared to control EGFP infections (0/18) (Figure S6B). The most commonly observed defect following kazald1 overexpression was syndactyly (8/15 abnormal limbs), and other defects included missing digits, truncated digits, severe clinodactyly, and ectopic tissue growth on the palm and digits (Figure S6C). Our morpholino and retroviral experiments highlight a functional role for kazald1 during limb regeneration, as perturbing its expression during this process adversely affected the progression and outcome of limb regeneration. Another report also discovered enriched expression of kazald1 in a regenerative context in vitro (Athippozhy et al., 2014). However, in this study, the expression of the transcript was not proﬁled in intact or regenerating limbs, and the bulk of the expression was attributed to nerves. Here we show that the blastema cells themselves produce large amounts of kazald1 transcript. More studies will be needed to determine whether blastema cells are stimulated by the ingrowing regenerating nerve ﬁbers to upregulate this transcript.

Comparison of Tissues at Different Anatomical Locations Identiﬁes Candidate Transcripts of Positional Memory along Intact and Limb Regeneration Sites Axolotl limb tissues maintain a ‘‘positional memory’’ throughout life allowing for the precise regeneration of only lost limb elements following amputation, suggesting that speciﬁc genes may be differentially expressed along the length of the limb and control positional memory. To uncover such genes, we assayed samples of similar tissue type but of diverse positional/

anatomical context. First, we proﬁled cartilage from the wrist (carpals) and the ends of long bones (humerus, radius, and ulna). Second, we collected samples along the length of the limb, and blastemas arising from either proximal (mid-humerus) or distal (distal radius/ulna) amputations. We then analyzed their expression proﬁles to identify differentially expressed genes for each context. Arm Segments We performed two separate analyses to address the transcriptional differences between different locations along the proximal-distal axis of the arm (Figure 6). We ﬁrst performed pairwise comparisons to identify transcripts signiﬁcantly differentially expressed between any pair of arm segments. In the second approach, we performed analyses to uncover factors that show graded enrichment across the proximal-distal axis. Using the pairwise approach, we uncovered a relatively modest number of transcriptional differences between different segments of the forelimb (‘‘arm’’): 636 differentially expressed transcripts identiﬁed between at least one pair of arm segments and 83 transcripts involving all arm segments (Figures 6A and 6B; Table S5), especially in the hand (48/83). Many of these likely reﬂect differences in the cell-type composition of the different arm segments. For example, transcripts enriched in the forearm, elbow, and upper arm are also more highly enriched in skeletal muscle and bone tissue; transcripts enriched in upper arm are also enriched in bone and cartilage (Figure S7A). Interestingly, 27 of the 48 transcripts enriched in the hand relative to other arm segments are also hand speciﬁc relative to other non-arm tissues. These include keratins and other ﬁlamentous proteins (6/27) with known structural roles in skin, consistent with the increased surface area of the hand versus the rest of the arm. Notably, when comparing highly similar tissue types, we found little signal of position-speciﬁc expression. In particular, comparing cartilage between wrist and long bone, we found only minor distinctions (Figure S7B), such that the samples were very highly correlated (r = 0.98), with only 22 differentially expressed transcripts, mostly in lowly expressed or non-cartilage-speciﬁc genes. The arm segment analysis highlighted key transcripts with known function in limb polarity and candidates with uncharacterized functions in limb polarity (Figure 6B). First, we found hoxa13, which is known to mark distal elements in developing appendages (Haack and Gruss, 1993). Second, we found and validated a speciﬁc keratin, krt17, as exclusively expressed in the hand, restricted to the tubercles on the ventral/palmar surface of the hand (Figures 6B and 6C). Additional hand-enriched transcripts include a homolog of alpha tectorin (tecta), which is required for hearing in mammals (reviewed in Legan et al., 2014). Finally, one of the few transcripts that distinguishes upper-arm segments from other segments of intact limbs encodes a predicted ortholog of Chordin-like 1 (crdl1) (Figure 6B), a diffusible morphogen (reviewed in Zakin and De Robertis, 2010).
